strengths: The combination of adversarially generated training problems, bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets, and learned initializations is well motivated and potentially useful for repeatedly solving OT problems with fixed cost and dimension.

The Hilbert projective loss appropriately handles the potentials’ additive ambiguity. Proposition 4.3 provides a sound residual-to-solution error bound under positive-kernel assumptions, motivating the use of inexpensive refinement targets.

The marginal-feasibility results demonstrate substantial acceleration across four unseen image datasets. For CIFAR, Table 2 reports 3 iterations to reach 0.01 marginal violation, versus 47 with uniform initialization and 17 with Gaussian initialization.

The evaluation includes five independent training runs for the main curves, 500 test instances per dataset, a generator-versus-noise ablation, and timing results. Architecture descriptions, hyperparameters, and a public code link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central accuracy metric is inconsistently defined. Algorithm 1 returns <C, Γ>, whereas Section 5.2 defines the reference value as the minimum of <C, Γ> − εH(Γ). These quantities differ even at convergence. The manuscript must clarify which quantity the experiments actually measure before the reported percentage errors can support the claimed entropic-objective accuracy. Moreover, the one-iteration plans retain marginal violations, so accurate scalar predictions alone do not establish the claimed standalone solver quality.

The universality claim exceeds the theoretical support. Theorem 4.1 requires equal input/output dimensions and a global Lipschitz constraint, while the implemented generator maps 392 latent coordinates to 1,568 outputs and does not enforce that constraint. The authors acknowledge these differences but still use the theorem to rule out generator expressiveness as a bottleneck. Even full support for a hypothetical generator would not establish adequate training coverage or uniform accuracy of the learned predictor.

Theorem 4.1 also needs mathematical corrections. For example, q(z) = ReLU(λz) satisfies its assumptions but places positive probability mass at zero, so the output does not have the asserted ordinary density everywhere and q⁻¹ is not defined there. The proof cannot simply discard ReLU on the boundary, and Lipschitz continuity alone does not justify invoking differentiability everywhere. An interior almost-everywhere density statement or a full-support statement is repairable, but differs from the theorem presented.

The closest learned baseline, Amos et al. (2022), is explicitly excluded based on an untested assertion that it fails out of distribution. Comparing its learning objective under matched synthetic training data and computational budgets would help establish what the proposed generator and bootstrapping contribute. The noise ablation does not resolve this comparison, and the broad claim of being the first meta neural OT solver is insufficiently distinguished from this cited prior work.

The generator update lacks a convincing optimization justification. Its target depends on the generated marginals, yet Algorithm 2 stops gradients through that target. Consequently, the update need not ascend the actual recomputed residual objective. Proposition 4.3 relates residual values to potential error; it does not establish that this update generates harder problems or that the coupled training converges.

The experiments establish transfer among image datasets on one 28×28 grid with one cost and ε = 0.01, rather than accuracy for arbitrary marginals within that setting. Concentrated, sparse, and other challenging synthetic distributions would directly test the broader claim. Practical validation is also incomplete: Figure 8 omits Gaussian-initialization timing, while reference-solver tolerances, GPU timing procedures, and treatment of zero test masses are unspecified. These gaps limit confidence in the standalone-accuracy and runtime conclusions despite the convincing iteration reductions.
